intro: Two granola bars sit side by side with the same green box, the same oats on the front and the same price, and one has four times the added sugar of the other. A family's grocery money gets cut and someone has to make a week of dinners out of $200 and a half bag of rice. A friend with a peanut allergy is coming to dinner. Every one of these is a nutrition problem, and none of them is solved by knowing that vegetables are good for you. They are solved by reading a label, costing a menu and planning a week.

The first chapter is the science. You will learn the six nutrient classes, what each one does in the body and roughly how many calories a gram of each carries, the five MyPlate groups and the difference between a serving and a portion, and then the Nutrition Facts label line by line: serving size, calories, the percent Daily Value shortcut, sodium, added sugars and the ingredient list. You will finish with the nine major allergens the law requires on every label, what diabetes and a vegetarian diet change about a plan, and why water is the everyday drink.

The second chapter is the plan. You will take inventory, read the sale flyer, write a menu that balances across the day, cook once to eat twice, write a list by store section, compute a unit price, choose a store brand, cost a week against a labeled example budget, store what you bought at the safe temperatures, get dinner out of the pantry in fifteen minutes, and cut the waste that quietly eats a fifth of the food money. By the end you will be able to feed a household well for a week on paper before a single dollar is spent.
bigQuestion: How do you turn what you know about nutrients into a week of meals that a real family can afford, cook and actually eat?

timeline.t: Fannie Farmer's Boston Cooking-School Cook Book opens by defining food as anything that nourishes the body
The Pure Food and Drug Act makes it illegal to sell misbranded or adulterated food in the United States
Casimir Funk coins the word "vitamine" for the vital substances missing in deficiency diseases
The first Recommended Dietary Allowances are published in the United States
The USDA's Basic Seven food guide helps families eat well under wartime rationing
The Basic Four food groups replace the Basic Seven
The FDA sets up the first voluntary nutrition labeling on packaged food
The Nutrition Labeling and Education Act requires nutrition labels on most packaged food
The Food Guide Pyramid is released
The Nutrition Facts label appears on packages in its standard form
MyPlate replaces the pyramid with a picture of a plate divided into food groups
The label is redesigned with larger calories, updated serving sizes and a new Added Sugars line

words.d: a substance in food the body needs; the six classes are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water
a unit of food energy; carbohydrate and protein give about 4 per gram, fat about 9
a plant carbohydrate the body cannot digest; slows digestion, helps fullness and keeps food moving
the USDA picture guide: half the plate fruits and vegetables, half grains and protein foods, dairy on the side
the standard amount on the Nutrition Facts label that every number on the panel describes
the share of a day's amount of a nutrient in one serving; 5% or less is low, 20% or more is high
sugars put into a food in processing, listed on their own label line; Daily Value 50 g
milk, eggs, fish, shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame, which labels must name
the list of food already on hand in the refrigerator, freezer and pantry, where a meal plan starts
price divided by amount, such as cents per ounce, used to compare sizes and brands
cooking a large amount once so it covers two or more meals; leftovers kept three to four days
40 to 140 °F, where bacteria grow fastest; perishable food is refrigerated within two hours

test.q: Which nutrient class gives about 9 calories per gram?
test.why: Fat gives about 9 calories per gram; carbohydrate and protein give about 4; vitamins and minerals give none.

test.q: What is the body's main source of energy?
test.why: Carbohydrates are broken into glucose, the fuel that muscles and the brain burn first.

test.q: On MyPlate, what fills about half the plate?
test.why: Fruits and vegetables fill about half; grains and protein foods fill the other half; dairy sits beside the plate.

test.q: A label reads 250 calories per serving, 3 servings per container. Eating the whole container is about how many calories?
test.why: Every label number is per serving; 250 times 3 is 750.

test.q: Using the FDA rule, a food with 25% DV sodium per serving is:
test.why: Twenty percent or more of the Daily Value is high; 5% or less is low.

test.q: Which label line separates a sweetened yogurt from a plain one?
test.why: Plain yogurt has natural milk sugar but zero added sugars; the Added Sugars line shows sugar put in during processing.

test.q: Which of these must a U.S. food label name as a major allergen?
test.why: The nine major allergens are milk, eggs, fish, shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame.

test.q: A friend is having a severe allergic reaction with a tightening throat. What is the right response?
choices: Use their epinephrine auto-injector and call 911
test.why: Anaphylaxis requires epinephrine right away and a 911 call even if the injector seems to work.

test.q: Ingredients on a label are listed in what order?
test.why: The ingredient present in the largest amount by weight comes first; if sugar is in the first three, the food is sweet.

test.q: What is the first step in planning a week of meals?
choices: Take inventory of what is already in the kitchen
Choose a dessert for each night
test.why: Food on hand is already paid for; the menu and list are built from the inventory and the sale flyer.

test.q: Oats: 18 oz for $3.60 or 42 oz for $5.88. Which is cheaper per ounce?
choices: The 18 oz, at 20 cents an ounce
The 42 oz, at 14 cents an ounce
The 18 oz, because the total is lower
test.why: $3.60 ÷ 18 = 20 cents per ounce; $5.88 ÷ 42 = 14 cents per ounce.

test.q: Why do store brands usually cost less than name brands?
choices: They are lower quality by law
The store does not pay for national advertising
test.why: Store brands skip national marketing costs; for basics, the Nutrition Facts and ingredients are often the same.

test.q: A big pot of chili was just cooked for meals through midweek. How should it be stored?
choices: Divided into shallow containers and refrigerated within two hours
Left on the stove overnight to cool
Put in the refrigerator whole and hot with the lid on
Left on the counter with the lid off
test.why: Shallow containers cool through quickly, and the two-hour rule keeps the chili out of the 40 to 140 °F danger zone.

test.q: How many days can cooked leftovers stay in a refrigerator at or below 40 °F?
test.why: USDA guidance is three to four days for cooked leftovers; freeze anything you will not eat in time.

test.q: Which is a safe way to thaw frozen chicken for tomorrow's dinner?
choices: In a sink of hot water
test.why: Refrigerator thawing keeps the chicken at or below 40 °F the whole time; the counter and hot water put it in the danger zone.

write.prompt: Plan seven dinners for a household of four with a labeled example budget of $200 for the week. Write the inventory you start from, the menu with a protein, grain and vegetable for each night, a cost sheet with example prices for every ingredient you buy, and a storage plan for leftovers. Explain why each choice is there, including one unit-price comparison and one cook-once-eat-twice pair.
tips: Start with the inventory and put foods that expire soon in the first days.
Show the arithmetic on the cost sheet and check the total against $200 twice.
Name the safe temperature or time rule for every leftover and every raw meat.
Check one full day against MyPlate and say where each group shows up.
Label every price as an example.
